newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Taiwan non-negotiable for China, says Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan non-negotiable for China, says Singapore.

text.p: Singapore Defence Minister Tony Tan said on Wednesday the United States must understand that China is willing to go to war if Taiwan declares independence.

Tan, who is also a deputy prime minister, told Reuters in an interview that issues of human rights, bitter trade disputes and violations of intellectual property rights would not lead to a break in ties between Washington and Beijing.
"But China will go to war if Taiwan declares independence. This is an issue that must be made very clear," Tan said.

"This is an issue that is non-negotiable for China. The Taiwanese also know that the U.S. is the only superpower left in the world and the only one that can possibly help Taiwan to gain independence."
Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui does not advocate independence but his bid to raise Taiwan's diplomatic profile to complement its economic dynamism has stung the communist leadership on the mainland.
Beijing considers Taiwan a renegade province since the civil war separated them in 1949.

Washington severed diplomatic ties with Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government in switching recognition to Beijing in 1979 but maintains close unofficial links to the island and reserves a right to arm and defend Taiwan.

Tensions soared last March when Chinese war games and missile tests in waters off Taiwan loomed over the island's first presidential election, prompting the United States to send two aircraft carrier battlegroups into the area.
This fuelled Beijing's suspicions that other powers like the United States were backing what the communist government regards as Nationalist-ruled Taiwan's moves towards independence.
Tan said the picture was being complicated by the strong support Taiwan enjoys in the U.S. Congress.

He said there were some U.S. lawmakers who were "very sympathetic" to Taiwan's drive to gain more international recognition, including its aspiration to seek an independent seat in the United Nations.

"If China can be reassured by the United States that it adheres firmly to the one-China policy and will not assist any moves to Taiwanese independence, then I think that the other issues like trade, human rights, (and) intellectual property can be resolved," Tan added.
The relationship between China and the United States would determine the stability of Asia, home to the world's fastest growing economies.

"China has some apprehension that the U.S. is seeking to develop a containment strategy to slow down China's growth and curb its influence. The U.S., on the other hand, is wary about China developing as a great power," Tan said.
The two countries nearly started a trade war over U.S. charges of inadequate protection for intellectual property and are now embroiled in a dispute over Chinese textile exports.
